content: Zinc sulfide, also known as zinc sulphide, is a chemical compound with the molecular formula ZnS. It typically appears as a white to yellow-colored powder or crystal. The compound is most commonly found in its stable cubic form, which is also referred to as the mineral sphalerite. Additionally, it can exist in a hexagonal form, which is recognized both as a synthetic material and as the mineral wurtzite. Both sphalerite and wurtzite are intrinsic semiconductors with wide band gaps. Sphalerite has a melting point of 1991 Kelvin. The enthalpy of fusion for this compound is approximately 6 kJ/mol at 298 Kelvin. Zinc sulfide has been historically significant in the field of nuclear physics. It was utilized by Ernest Rutherford and other early researchers as a scintillation detector due to its ability to emit light when excited by X-rays or electron beams. This property made it valuable for applications such as X-ray screens and cathode ray tubes. Furthermore, zinc sulfide exhibits phosphorescence when exposed to blue or ultraviolet light, a phenomenon caused by impurities within the material. When doped with small amounts of suitable activators (in the range of parts per million), zinc sulfide serves as a phosphor in various applications. These include cathode ray tubes, X-ray screens, and glow-in-the-dark products. For instance, doping with silver results in a bright blue emission with a peak wavelength of 450 nm. Manganese doping produces an orange-red emission around 590 nm, while copper doping provides a long-lasting glow with the characteristic greenish color commonly associated with glow-in-the-dark materials. Copper-doped zinc sulfide (ZnS:Cu) is also employed in electroluminescent panels. Zinc sulfide is further used as an infrared optical material, capable of transmitting light from visible wavelengths to beyond 12 micrometers. It can be manufactured as planar optical windows or shaped into lenses. The material is produced in microcrystalline sheets through the reaction of hydrogen sulfide gas with zinc vapor. This form, known as FLIR (Forward Looking Infrared) grade ZnS, appears as a pale, milky yellow, visibly opaque material. When subjected to hot isostatic pressing (HIP), this material can be transformed into a water-clear form marketed under the trademark Cleartran. Earlier commercial versions were sold under the name Irtran-2, though this designation is now obsolete. Zinc sulfide is unique among II-VI semiconductors in that it can be doped to function as either an n-type or p-type semiconductor. Structurally, it is a covalently bonded solid. In laboratory settings, zinc sulfide can be synthesized by mixing zinc and sulfur in appropriate proportions and igniting the mixture. As the reaction subsides, zinc sulfide is formed. However, this process is highly hazardous and requires careful handling to mitigate risks.
